title: A superheterodyne receiver signal path, stage by stage
summary: How one 1930s idea still pulls a station out of the air: mix every signal to one fixed frequency, then do all the hard work there.

blocks.title: Move every station to one address, then answer it
blocks.body: Tuning the whole dial is easy. The hard parts of a receiver - pulling a weak station out of noise and rejecting the loud one next door - are far easier at a single, fixed frequency. The superheterodyne idea is to convert whatever you want to hear into that one frequency, and invest all the cleverness there.

items.label: Where nearly all gain and selectivity live

blocks.heading: The signal path, end to end

nodes.title: Antenna
nodes.detail: Every station in town arrives at once, plus noise.

nodes.title: RF stage
nodes.detail: Light amplification and a first, loose filter that tracks the dial.

nodes.title: Mixer
nodes.detail: Combines the signal with the local oscillator; outputs sum and difference frequencies.

nodes.title: IF filter
nodes.detail: Keeps only the difference frequency - the intermediate frequency. This is where selectivity happens.

nodes.title: IF amplifier
nodes.detail: Most of the radio's gain, at one fixed frequency where great amplifiers are easy to build.

nodes.title: Detector
nodes.detail: Recovers the audio from the IF - the information leaves the carrier here.

nodes.title: Audio stage
nodes.detail: Volume and power for the speaker or headphones.

blocks.heading: The trick, in one move
blocks.body: Multiply two sinusoids and you get their sum and their difference. The local oscillator is tuned to sit exactly one IF above the station you want. Whatever station that is, the mixer drops it onto the same IF - 455 kHz in a classic AM set. Tune the dial and the LO moves with it, so the difference never changes. The rest of the radio is built once, for one frequency, and built well.

blocks.heading: A worked pass through the dial
rows: The carrier you asked the dial for
Always the station plus the IF (high-side injection)
1455 plus 455 - an unwanted station here also lands on the IF
Its difference is 445 kHz, outside the IF filter's passband
blocks.caption: One station converts to 455 kHz. Everything else misses the filter and goes nowhere.

blocks.title: The image is the design's one shadow
blocks.body: A station at the LO frequency plus the IF also mixes down to the same 455 kHz - the image. The RF stage's loose tracking filter exists mostly to kill it before the mixer. This is why better receivers use a higher first IF: the farther the image sits from the wanted station, the easier it is to filter out.

blocks.heading: Follow one song from air to speaker
items: A 1000 kHz carrier, amplitude-modulated with music, lands on the antenna microvolts tall.
The RF stage lifts it a little and rejects 1910 kHz, the image.
The mixer combines it with 1455 kHz from the LO; the difference is 455 kHz, music intact.
The IF filter keeps a tight window around 455 kHz and dumps the adjacent stations.
IF amplifiers boost the signal a million-fold, at a frequency chosen to make that easy.
The detector strips the carrier and hands the music to the audio stage.
The audio stage drives the speaker. The song arrives.

blocks.heading: The quiet feedback loop
blocks.body: The detector also produces a voltage proportional to signal strength, fed backward to turn down the IF and RF gain on strong stations. That automatic gain control is why a weak distant station and a local blowtorch both come out of the speaker at a civilized volume, and why the tuning meter - if the radio has one - moves with signal strength.

blocks.heading: Why 455 kHz specifically
blocks.body: Low enough that stable, selective filters and huge gain are cheap; high enough that the image sits far enough away to filter. Every IF is this same compromise. FM broadcast chose 10.7 MHz for wider channels; many modern receivers use two or three conversions, stepping down through a high first IF for image rejection and a low final IF for selectivity.

blocks.heading: Check the path
blocks.prompt: Where does a superheterodyne receiver get most of its ability to reject the station 10 kHz away?
options: The IF filter, working at one fixed frequency
The audio stage, by filtering treble
blocks.explanation: Adjacent-channel rejection is the IF filter's job. Because every station is converted to the same IF, one excellent fixed filter does the work for the whole dial - that is the entire point of the architecture.

blocks.heading: Check the arithmetic
blocks.prompt: An AM receiver with a 455 kHz IF is tuned to 1200 kHz using high-side injection. Where is its local oscillator?
options: 1655 kHz - the station plus the IF
745 kHz - the station minus the IF
blocks.explanation: With high-side injection the LO sits one IF above the wanted station: 1200 + 455 = 1655 kHz. The mixer difference lands on 455 kHz no matter where the dial points.
